summary: The note examines how public information and media relations were handled during power and service outages on the Eastern Seaboard starting 14 September 2023. Social media became the main channel for real-time updates but also spread misinformation, while mobile network failures left some hard-hit people without access. Official spokespersons, joint press conferences, a Federal Communications Commission (FCC) review of Wireless Emergency Alerts, and feedback efforts are presented as keys to future resilience.
one_line: Analysis of social media, misinformation, mobile network reliability and spokesperson trust in communications during the September 2023 Eastern Seaboard outages.
key_facts: Power and service outages struck the Eastern Seaboard starting from 14 September 2023, disrupting cities including New York and Boston.
Facebook, Twitter and newer platforms like TikTok became lifelines for real-time updates, heavily supplementing or superseding radio and television broadcasts.
Johnathan Andrews, spokesperson for the Department of Public Safety, said social media lets authorities broadcast crucial information swiftly to a broad audience.
Power companies such as Eastern Grid used Twitter handles to share updates on power restoration, anticipated recovery times and safety advice.
On October 2, 2023, an unaffiliated Twitter account inaccurately reported a total grid failure scheduled to last for weeks, causing panic among affected residents.
Sociologist Dr. Emilia Chen said social media is indispensable in crises but also a vector for panic and falsehoods, creating an 'infodemic' authorities must manage.
Twitter's misinformation labels were used, but their effectiveness remains a subject of ongoing analysis and debate.
Cellular networks showed varying reliability during the outages and failed altogether in some areas; mobile cell towers were rapidly deployed to boost capacity.
Telecommunications expert Laura Jenkins called reliance on mobile services during outages a 'double-edged sword' because of congestion and infrastructure damage.
On September 21, Mayor Stephanie Rawlings of Baltimore and energy sector leadership held a joint press conference streamed live across multiple social platforms.
Media relations expert Martin Greene stressed that the public looks for a trusted leader and that a consistent, calm authority figure helps maintain order.
On October 7, the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) announced a review of the Wireless Emergency Alerts (WEA) system, noting direct alerts to mobile devices can reach wider audiences faster.
Jessica Martell heads the new Emergency Communication Task Force, and city councils and utility companies have been gathering resident feedback on their outage experiences.
The note concludes that access to reliable information is as much a utility as electricity itself.
